music.cue: Enters under the hook, drops to half level under scenes S3-S5, swells slightly under S6, fades out under the outro.

scenes.narration: The Justice Department just told California's election officials: count the wrong ballots, and you could be prosecuted.
scenes.visual: Pixel-art Justice Department building at night; a stack of letters flies out toward a map of California lighting up county by county.

scenes.narration: On Friday, federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California, at least 18 counties by one count, nearly every county by others, ordering them to set aside flagged mail ballots within 48 hours. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli warned that any official who knowingly processes a noncitizen's ballot is opening themselves to legal jeopardy.
scenes.on_screen_text: Oct 23 · 18 to 57 of 58 counties (reports differ) · 48 hours
scenes.visual: Pixel-art Bill Essayli standing at a podium, pointing at a row of county clerks behind their desks.

scenes.narration: It started in Los Angeles. The Justice Department says 20,000 noncitizens were sent mail ballots in California. It gave the county and Secretary of State Shirley Weber 48 hours to review its list, then sued to stop those ballots from being counted. A hearing is set for Tuesday.
scenes.on_screen_text: Oct 13: 48-hour demand · Oct 15: lawsuit · Oct 27: hearing
scenes.visual: Pixel-art timeline along a courthouse steps; a thumb drive with a sticky note on top of an LA County desk.

scenes.narration: California officials push back. Weber called it an emergency of the DOJ's creation and said the list lacks the detail to be useful. Los Angeles County checked a sample of 200 names and found nearly 40 percent were born in the United States.
scenes.visual: Pixel-art Shirley Weber at a desk signing a letter; a bar chart of the 200-name sample.

scenes.narration: Inside the U.S., the split is sharp. The administration and its Republican allies say federal records found likely noncitizens on the rolls and that officials must act now. California's election administrators call the list unverified and the letters intimidation. Congressional Democrats say it's an attempt to interfere with the November 3rd election.
scenes.on_screen_text: Verify now · Unverified list · Election interference
scenes.visual: Three pixel-art groups on a split screen, each under its own banner; no real faces.

scenes.narration: Abroad, outlets that covered it frame the push as federal overreach built on shaky data, while Canadian coverage ties it to a separate U.S.-Canada fight over election interference. And the administration has reportedly asked an appeals court to step in before Tuesday's hearing.
scenes.on_screen_text: World: "overreach on shaky data" · Canada: a separate interference row
scenes.visual: Pixel-art globe with speech bubbles from the UK, Europe, the Middle East and Canada.

scenes.narration: Still unknown: how many counties got the letters, what the judge will decide, and how the federal list was built. Sources are in the description.
scenes.on_screen_text: Unknown: county count · court ruling · DHS method
